schema: principle: id, statement (own words), applies_to, operation, check, source {book, pages}, status, reviewer

principles.statement: Ease is a fixed amount added at each body measurement, not a shape change.
Front and back side seams and shoulder seams must correspond in length after any change.
The armhole is a separate curve drafted from set points. Changes to width or waist should not reshape it.
For knit tops the book starts from a dartless foundation rather than shaping the waist with darts.
When a side-seam width change is uneven, the front takes one quarter of the side change and the back takes one half.
Side seams of sleeveless tops may rise higher at the underarm than side seams of tops with sleeves.
A slash or pivot change is tapered out to nothing at a seam, crease or hipline, so the new line blends into the original.
Order of work for a bust fit: adjust width first, then armscye and side seam, then waist darts.
When only the back is too long, shorten the back alone with a parallel tuck, and widen the back dart by the same amount.
Make alterations in this order: length changes first (even, then uneven, then combined), then width changes (even, then uneven, then combined).
Asymmetric alterations are blended out to nothing at the pattern centre, and dart tips keep the same height from the floor.
Corresponding dartlines and seamlines must be the same length after an alteration.
Centre lines and side seams meet hemlines at right angles, centre edges are straight, and side edges below the fullest body bulge are straight.
Waistlines, necklines and armscye seams form a continuous smooth line where they meet side seams, shoulders and underarms.
Sleeve cap seams are about 3/4 to 1 inch larger than the bodice armscye they fit, to allow for movement.
Work on a pressed, flat pattern with the printed side up, and mark alteration lines clearly. No puckers or wrinkles may remain after an alteration.
A change to one edge must be matched by equal amounts at the stitching line of each adjoining edge, otherwise the pieces will not join.
Centre front and centre back stay straight. Seams that meet them meet at right angles, and length changes there are spread evenly about 7.5-10 cm from the centre.
Plan the alteration in the area nearest the edge that needs change, which keeps distortion to a minimum.
Clip into the seam allowance to form hinges, but do not cut through the stitching line.
When a change is both even and uneven, make the even part first, then pivot the remaining section so the edges align.
The pivot method duplicates the area to be altered, moves the duplicate, and traces the new cutting line, so the new edge keeps the original contour.
For an asymmetric figure, the altered half is tapered back to the original at centre back or centre front, so the two halves join at the centre line.
Ease depends on the fabric. A design made for stretch fabric has some ease removed, and the same design in woven fabric will be too tight at bust, upper arm and hip.
Each outer layer (interlining, lining, outer garment) is cut slightly larger than the layer beneath, so the layers lie smoothly over one another.
Heavier, bulkier fabric needs more ease than light fabric in the same style.
A garment must look balanced both side to side and top to bottom. Symmetrical balance is equal on each side of the centre line; asymmetrical balance needs equal visual weight.
A garment should have one dominant point of interest, with others subordinate. Attention can be moved away from a figure variation by a stronger detail.
Some fit problems are solved by choosing or modifying the style, such as omitting a shoulder pad on a square shoulder, rather than altering the pattern.

Assume each side of the body is a mirror of the other only until measured. Asymmetry is common and must be checked for each area: neck slope, shoulder length and height, back and chest width, bust, waist, hip, and limbs.

Standard proportions give a starting reference: back neck-to-waist about equal to shoulder width; hip about equal to or slightly less than shoulder width; bust about equal to hip; waist about ten inches less than bust.
Check posture before altering, because posture can cause many fit problems that correct themselves when posture changes. Rounded upper backs and swayed backs change the length of the back and front.
Choose the starting pattern size from bust circumference measured at scye level. A larger cup on a small frame may need the next size up, and the armhole and shoulders then need checking.
Check posture against a wall: shoulders alone touching means overly erect, buttocks alone means swayed back, and shoulder blades and buttocks touching with a gap at the waist means slumped.
Pattern companies draft different default proportions (back length, shoulder slope, dart placement, sleeve cap). Choose the company whose defaults need the fewest alterations for the figure.
Centre back and centre front seams should hang perpendicular to the floor and sit centred on the body. Use this as a visual check after making up.
The side seam should slope slightly forward from the underarm. A side seam that drops straight, or slopes back, is a fit sign to check.
A dart should point toward the crown of the curve it shapes and end about 1 inch (2.5 cm) short of the fullest part of that curve.
The waistline should be parallel to the floor and follow the body contour. A waistline that tilts or floats away from the body is a fit sign.
The back neckline should cross through the most prominent vertebra at the base of the neck. Check this point when setting the back neck.
The shoulder seam should lie close to the body and look visually straight from the neck to the armscye.
The armscye should sit about ½ inch (1.25 cm) from the outer surface of the arm and line up with the back and front arm creases.
The outer edge of a sleeve should extend about ½ inch beyond the armscye, to give movement at the top of the arm.
The sleeve underarm seam should line up with the centre of the wrist when the arm is hanging.
The basic ease a garment needs depends on its style. Strapless and sleeveless designs need little; sportswear needs more than business wear.
Flare appears where the fabric is on the bias. Changing the grain angle on the pattern moves where the flare falls.
On a symmetrical flared garment, the ripples on each side should match in size and start at the same height.
Stitched pleats and tucks lie smooth without tension. Enough ease is needed so pleats and vents stay closed when standing.
Gathers that lie on the body fall softly over bulges without tension, and need enough lengthwise ease for movement.
Gathers that stand away from the body need added length. The amount depends on the edge contour, the ratio of gathered to flat area, and the grain direction of the seam.

Draped fabric holds its shape only with the right tension. Too little ease in a gathered or folded area produces diagonal folds. Draped edges must be cut and matched accurately and fitted on the body.
Darts should form smooth, flowing lines. On a large curve, two or more narrow darts fit better than one large dart. Darts should not emphasise a body variation.
A collar stand fits smoothly at the back of the neck, keeps a continuous roll line, and is in proportion to the neck length.
If the neckline curve or shoulder slope changes, the collar must change too. On uneven shoulders the collar point drops on the low side unless the collar is altered.
The outer layer of a rolled collar or lapel is cut slightly larger than the layers beneath and eased into place, to prevent distortion.
Pocket position and size are checked at the first fitting, before the pockets are applied.
A pocket over a body curve needs ease to lie flat, and flaps and outer layers are made slightly larger than the layers beneath.
Fitting needs a full-length mirror, space to walk several steps from it, good plain lighting, a chair and a standing-height table, so the whole figure and garment are visible.
Wear the same underwear and shoes during fitting as will be worn with the finished garment, so that darts and ease are not changed later.
Use the standard 5/8 inch (1.5 cm) seam allowance. Wide allowances on curved edges such as the armscye and neck cause problems.
Start from a basic pattern with a close-fitting neck, standard armscye, waist and straight skirt, so the fabric requirements are determined for all body areas.
When a stitching line changes in length, the matching line on the adjoining piece must change by the same amount. A position-only change needs no adjoining length change.
Fit the simplest garment part first (skirt, trousers, bodice, sleeves) and start each garment unit at the largest area where fabric touches the body.
Once the garment is on, fix length problems before circumference problems, and adjust the hem last.
To check the circumference, subtract the chart measurement from the body measurement at waist, hip and bust, divide each difference by four (four seam edges), and apply it parallel to the side seam.

To check the sleeve, add 1 to 2 inches (2.5 to 5 cm) to the biceps measurement, subtract from the sleeve pattern about 2 inches below the cap, halve the difference, and apply it parallel to the underarm seam.
Fit the garment right side out with closures pinned accurately and the garment centre lines in line with the body centres. Work side to side in the same area.
A side or shoulder seam can move to change how front and back read without changing total size: let out one side and take up the other by an equal amount.

Body variations often counterbalance each other (for example, a rounded shoulder with a hollow chest). Look for the related variation before altering, and adjust only the distorted side when the difference is slight.

Wrinkle direction shows the fault: horizontal tension means too small circumference; loose horizontal folds mean too long; vertical tension means too short; loose vertical, diagonal or puffy folds mean the dart is too wide; tight diagonal wrinkles mean the dart is too narrow.
A garment needs no change when its measurements and shape equal the body plus ease. Where the garment differs, change the length or width of that part.

A dart-equivalent seam forms along each body slope. The larger the bulge or the steeper the slope, the larger the dart. Asymmetric halves need darts that differ, with tips level and at equal distances from the centre.
Describe needed changes by the body shape they respond to, in logical sequence, so the pattern alteration is easier to repeat.
Slash-and-spread (or lap) and pivot-slide are the two common alteration methods. Slash is for trial fitting; pivot moves the stitching line and suits fashion garments.
Evaluate the total fit by moving as the garment will be worn: stand, sit, walk, bend, stoop and raise the arms. The garment should return to a correct position without help.
Alter the pattern with the same method used on the garment: slash, pivot, or seam (moving the seam allowance).

In the pinned pattern method, do not pin seam allowances facing each other outward (the body looks larger) or turned toward the body (the pattern looks tighter). Overlap the allowances with stitching lines coinciding, or turn one under along the non-darted curve.

Paper patterns are semi-rigid. A larger figure makes the pattern look tight and the edge ripple, rather than letting the grain bow as fabric does. Judge fabric fit with a fabric check, not paper alone.
For each unit, place narrow fitting bands at the scye, waist and fullest hip, mark centre front and back on the bands, and pin the pattern's centre lines to those marks.
Fit the sleeve last: keep the bodice pinned, slide the sleeve onto a relaxed arm, and match the cap to the armscye at the notches before pinning the top to the shoulder line.
When cutting to adjust, slash as near the closest affected seamline as possible, and note the location and amount.
Evaluate hem position at an attractive place on the figure and coordinate hems on all pinned units so the proportions are related.
Dart lines should point toward the bulge and stop about 1 inch (2.5 cm) short of its fullest part, with centres on body centres and tissue smooth.
Pin strips of tissue or lightly fuse backing under slashed-and-spread areas so the opening holds its shape.
For learning to fit, use a plain-weave muslin of medium weight with balanced threads, pliable but firm enough to resist distortion.
Cut the basic trial garment without adjustment to find body variations; the adjusted basic then becomes part of the pattern for every later garment.
On a trial garment, mark all stitching lines, centre front and back, and crosswise lines at the hip, chest, blade and sleeve cap, so left and right amounts can be compared.
Pin-baste for the first fit of simple styles and hand-baste complex ones. Do not let the machine push or feed the fabric; long threads and sharp needles keep the grain true.
Press the basted trial garment and keep it together for later fittings.
On a trial garment, figure variations show as tilted, bowed, sagging or strained grain, which reveals what needs changing.
If a trial garment is cut apart to make a pattern, align each piece on the grain before copying, or the copy will distort.

Block fabric so the yarns cross at 90 degrees, fold lengthwise, match edges and selvages at right angles, and press along the lengthwise grain. Pin the pattern on grain, cut smoothly, and transfer grain and fitting lines.
Fit the simplest unit first, refine it, then join it to the next unit. Join pieces exactly on stitching lines and press darts and seams before crossing them.
If possible, plan a centre-front opening for fitting, so the garment can be put on and taken off without disturbing basting.

A well-fitted garment has centres perpendicular to the floor on the body centres, dartlines aimed at the fullest part of the bulge, horizontal lines level, attractive edges, and smooth fabric with appropriate ease and no tightness.
After joining fitted units, refine the whole garment, then transfer every adjustment to the paper pattern if it will be reused.
For the measurement method, add ease to the body measurements of areas that move or expand, then compare the total with the pattern.
Body size changes through the day and with stance. Measure at a consistent time, with the person standing erect and relaxed, and recheck any reading that changes when the person turns or bends.
Measure the lower torso before the upper torso, and rest the person between sections so the readings stay accurate.

Take each measurement at the level the chart specifies (for example, side seam ¾ to 1 inch below the arm hinge, blade width 1 to 1¼ inches above the arm hinge), because the same measurement at a different level gives a different reading.
Record back and front circumferences separately, because the back measures the rib cage and the front includes bust or cup size.
When comparing to the pattern, exclude seam and hem allowances, darts, stitched pleats and tucks. Allow extra width for gathers, unstitched pleats and flare separately.
Skirt length equals the side-seam body length minus the desired hem height from the floor.
Mark the hip level 7 to 9 inches (18 to 23 cm) below the waist, or 1 to 1½ inches below the point where the side seam becomes straight, and draw the hipline parallel to the hemline.

Where centre length and hip depth differ from the pattern by the same amount, change length above the hipline. Where only the hip depth differs, change above the hipline and restore length at the hem. Where only the side or centre length differs, change at the hem.
Equal waist and hip width differences are corrected along the side seamline. Unequal differences are corrected at the side seam, a dart, or a style seam near the side.
For prominent front thighs, add width at the side of the pattern, or increase the waistline curve by moving part of the waist dart into the hem.
For close-fitting trousers, add about 1 to 1⅜ inches (2.5 to 3.5 cm) of length above the back waistline depth measurement.
For fitted trouser legs, change the kneeline to fit the knee position and keep the new hem length.
Where the inseam measurement ends on the body, mark a new hemline parallel to the original hem.
When the crotch length is still off after the length changes, split the remaining difference into thirds: one third to the front extension, two thirds to the back.
For close-fitting trousers, change knee, calf and instep measures in even amounts along the inseam and side seam, after checking for slits or plackets at the hem.
For a low neckline, take the centre length from the waist up to the maximum neckline depth rather than the neck.
Compare full bodice length parallel to the centre line. For a widened neckline, extend the shoulder line and measure about 2⅜ to 2¾ inches (6 to 7 cm) from the centre, parallel to it.
A princess line passes near but not over the bust point. Use the bust-height marks along the dart fold or the curve of the side panel to locate the bust level.
A jacket, coat, jumper or vest may have a lowered armscye to take a blouse underneath, so compare side seams with the outer garment's ease in mind.
When the bodice lengths (centre, full length, blade and bust heights) all differ by the same amount, change below the bustline.

Find the shoulder-tip width by squaring across from the extended centre line to the shoulder tip, then draw a line parallel to the centre through the marks. Jacket shoulders run wider than basic-bodice shoulders.
Add shoulder pad height and shoulder extension to the body measurement before comparing it with the pattern.

Decide which bodice change is needed by seeing which measurements agree. If the shoulder-tip measure agrees but the centre and bust-height measures differ by the same amount, change between scye and shoulder to alter armscye depth. If only the armhole-level measures differ, change at the shoulder and underarm to raise or lower the armhole.
If the back neck, shoulder and blade measures agree but the centre lengths differ, change at the neck and shoulder to alter centre lengths and the shoulder slope.

On empire styles, compare the chest and bust contour length from mid-shoulder to the empire seam; change the upper bodice at the empire line. On princess lines change at the bust level of both pieces.
Jackets carry more width ease than dresses. The shoulder can be extended ½ to ⅜ inch (1 to 1.5 cm); a wider neckline may shorten the shoulder by ⅛ inch (0.3 cm) or more.

Change bodice width at the place the measurements point to: the centre-to-dart line when all widths agree; the armscye when only the armscye width differs; the dart or princess when only the bust width differs; the side seam when only the waist width differs.

When the underarm and elbow-position measures both differ by the same amount, change the sleeve below the elbow. If only the underarm differs, change above the elbow. If only the elbow position differs, change below the elbow and restore the underarm length above it.
Adjust sleeve cap height to match the overarm length, after adding shoulder pad height to the body measurement.
Jacket sleeves are about 1 inch (2.5 cm) wider than dress sleeves, and coat sleeves about 2 inches (5 cm) wider, measured at the biceps.

When the biceps, elbow and wrist all differ by the same amount, change at the sleeve centre and underarm; if only the biceps differ, change above the elbow; if only the elbow differs, change the back underarm width and dart size.

If elbow rotation is noted, swing the front underarm seam forward until the wristline moves ½ to ¾ inch (1.2 to 1.8 cm), pivoting at elbow level, and keep the dart increase no more than that forward change.
A pattern must lie flat after any alteration, with no puckers, puffiness or wrinkles. If it does not, the change is wrong or the edge has not been trued.
When a centre line's length changes, keep the change even for about 3 to 4 inches (7.5 to 10 cm) from the centre so the centre line stays straight.
When a dart changes in length, position or size, fold it closed and cut along the pattern edge. The dart base then takes its correct shape.

For the slash method, cut through the interior in the area that the body needs changed. An even change runs across the whole area; a change on one seamline runs to where the variation tapers; an interior-only change runs from one stitching line to another, through the dart centres.
Clip across the seam allowance to create hinges, but do not cut the stitching line; the hinges let the pattern lie flat.
Move alterations by type: slide or overlap parallel for an even change; pivot the edge away from the interior to increase an uneven change, and onto the interior to decrease it.
For a change that is both even and uneven, make the even part first, then pivot the remaining section until the edges align.
The slash method distorts more the further the cut is from the pattern edge, and uneven slashes distort dart size and edge shape. Plan the cut near the edge that needs change.
In the seam method, free the seam allowance from the point where the variation starts, keep the interior uncut, and move the allowance to make the change.

In the seam method, place pivot points at the point of greatest variation, where the variation falls to nothing, where an even change becomes uneven, at the base of affected darts, and at affected corners.
The seam method keeps the grainline, darts and tucks undisturbed, distorts least, and suits several variations on one piece.

In the pivot method, trace the affected area and edge, move the duplicate by its pivot points, then trace the new cutting line in a contrasting colour. Match the first trace to the original cutting line, then true the edges.
When pivoting, draw the new cutting line in a colour that contrasts with the original, to avoid cutting the old line.
For asymmetric figures, alter each half of the pattern to its own needs. The changes taper into each other at centre back or centre front, so the centre line stays straight.
On both sides of a front or back pattern, keep the dart tips at the same height from the floor and at the same distance from centre, unless one breast or shoulder blade is significantly different.
A waist height change may be needed when a high hip is added at the side seam, and a bodice side seam may need to shorten to match.
For asymmetric figures, the aim is an illusion of symmetry, using style lines to camouflage changes that cannot be avoided.
Several variations on one piece are best handled by the seam or pivot method, because slashes overlap and distort when combined.
When a dart base changes, level the pattern across it so that corresponding dartline lengths stay equal.
Blend asymmetric alterations to nothing at the pattern centre, and keep waist dart tips the same height from the floor on both sides.
A personalised basic pattern records one person's measurements, shape and minimum ease, and is used to compare and alter fashion patterns.
Make the length changes in this order: even, uneven, then combined. Make width changes in the same order.

A hem length change is made by slashing below the hipline, by moving the hem allowance up to meet the alteration line, or by pivoting a new parallel hem. Keep centre lines straight and true the side seam across the hem.
When the waistline has an even-then-uneven change, adjust the dart widths so the waist circumference stays the same. Taper the change to nothing at the termination point.
When the hip width changes evenly then unevenly, spread evenly at the hip and taper to nothing at the termination point on the side seam, then true the hem corner.
When cutting an asymmetric garment, cut the duplicate pieces to the larger side and mark and trim the smaller side to its own pattern.
On a finished pattern, centre back, centre front and side seams meet the hemlines at right angles, and necklines and waistlines meet the centre lines at right angles.
The whole centre back and centre front edges must be straight, and the skirt side edges below the bulge must be straight.
The flare on skirt side seams below the fullest bulge must be the same on back and front.
Waistlines meet side seams, necklines meet shoulders, and armscyes meet the underarm and shoulder, each in a continuous smooth line.
A skirt or trouser waist edge is about ¼ inch (6 mm) larger than the waistband it attaches to.
The sleeve underarm seam spaces should be about ⅛ to ⅜ inch (3 to 9 mm) larger than the corresponding bodice armscye areas.
Back and front sleeve cap seams should each be about ¾ to 1 inch larger than the corresponding bodice armscye areas. The book's metric conversion does not match, so confirm before use.
Press paper patterns with a warm dry iron, because steam shrinks paper and excess heat shrinks backing; keep the iron off tape.

A sloper can be cut from the separated sections of an adjusted fitting garment. Mark seams, darts, centres and hems first, cut on the marks without stretching, and label each section with its changes.
When sloper sections are separated, leave a gap of about 1/16 inch (2 mm) between them, and tape both sides of each join so the sloper folds without tearing.
Cut dart interiors with straight lines on a sloper, because curved lines cannot be folded during design; curved darts can be stitched as curves later.
If a fashion pattern is the same brand, size and figure type as the basic, make the same adjustments to it, so the designer's fullness and design lines are kept.
A lowered or widened neckline can remove the need for a low-neck-base or high-neck-base change. Check the design edges before altering.
If the armscye is lowered, check the sleeve cap and the bodice bust width for enough ease.
If the shoulder tip looks too narrow or too wide against the basic, check the design for puffed sleeves or an extended shoulder line before altering.
To compare fashion and basic, match bodices at centre front, centre back and natural waist; match skirts the same way; match sleeve cutting lines at the underarm extension and the sleeve centre.

A fashion pattern must be at least as large as the basic in these areas: shoulder width and slope, chest and blade width, bust length and width, armhole depth and width, back and front waist lengths, waist, hip, crotch, thigh, skirt and trouser length, elbow dart position and long sleeve length.
Pretest a new design as a small-scale pattern and garment on a mannequin. A disappointing design is cheaper to correct at small scale.
Check that the sleeve cap fits the bodice armhole before notching. Notch the front and back armholes to match.
A sleeve crown needs about 1 to 2 cm of ease at its top. A flatter crown needs less ease; a higher crown needs more.
Jackets need extra ease at the bust, waist, hip, neck and arms so they can be worn over other garments. Build them from a blouse or dartless shirt foundation.
A double-breasted front needs much more centre-front overlap than a single-breasted one.
A slim darted blouse has about 10 cm of ease at the bust and 2.5 cm at the waist.
A dartless shirt drafted from the hip foundation suits only looser garments or knit fabric.
A skirt needs about 1.25 cm of ease at the hip and at the waist. An optional small centre-waist dart can replace the waistband ease.
Cutting a skirt on the bias softens its fall.
Several smaller back darts spread hip fullness across the hipline for a smoother fit than one dart.
Trousers need about 2 cm of ease at the hip and crotch depth plus about 2.5 cm.
Waist reduction figures for trousers are guidelines. Check the result against the actual waist measurement.
To slim a trouser leg, take in the seams in steps: more at the hem than at the knee, then blend back to the crotch.
Gathers, tucks or pleats in a yoke are the best way to add fullness to a bodice; panelling gives a slimmer fit.
Moving the bust dart into shoulder tucks keeps the basic fit; more fullness needs a slash through to the hem and a spread. Stop cuts short of their ends so the pieces stay joined.
A gathered edge is normally about twice the length of the edge it fits; less gives a looser gather, more gives extra fullness.
Make cross-marks where panels meet, so the joins can be matched after the panels are separated or spread.
Yokes in checked fabric look best cut on the bias; striped fabric is cut on the cross grain.
The fuller the gathers, the softer the fabric should be.
Princess lines give a slimming effect; the straight line suits dresses and tailored jackets, and the curved line accentuates the bust more.
For a closer fit on a princess-line garment, reshape the panels, especially under the bust curve.
A neckline must stay in proportion with the rest of the garment and with any collar or tie added to it.
Reduce a scoop neckline at the centre front by about 1 cm so it does not gape; scoops are reduced for a closer fit in general.
A cowl neck drapes only in a knit or a supple woven fabric.
A firm fabric suits a tie that keeps its shape; a soft fabric suits a jabot.
The softer the fabric, the fuller a frill must be.
An off-the-shoulder neckline is best suited to a slimmer figure.
On a halter neck, waist darts can be replaced with ease, and the centre front cut on the fold.
A flat collar sits over the neck seam when the shoulder seams are overlapped slightly, producing a small roll.
A mandarin collar needs extra neck ease; dropping the centre front about 1 cm gives it.
A notched collar is built from a roll line; the shoulder and collarstand are set from it, and matched shoulder widths are needed if a back facing is used.
A sleeve must leave enough room for the elbow to bend without strain and should hang straight, following the natural curve of the arm.
A single elbow dart gives a pointed elbow; dividing it into several darts curves the sleeve more gently.
Adding a cuff to a gathered sleeve shortens the sleeve by about half the cuff width.
On a puffed sleeve, spreading the crown gives fuller gathers and raising it gives a puffier shape.
A shirt sleeve with a cuff should be about 1.5 cm longer than the fitted sleeve, so it falls slightly over the cuff.
On a dropped shoulder, drop the armhole so the new armhole stays close in length to the regular armhole.
A two-piece sleeve follows the arm's natural curve by moving the hem forward at the elbow and curving the back elbow.
Use a two-piece raglan for rigid fabric, where a single dart would form a point; a raglan pad helps keep the shoulder curve.
Kimono and batwing sleeves are cut in one with the bodice, giving a T-shaped silhouette with soft folds.
A buttonstand is wide enough to leave about 1 cm from the button edge to the stand edge.
Place a button on the bustline so the garment does not gape.
The first buttonhole sits about 2.5 cm below the neck seam for a tidy collar.
For a fuller fit, add the same amount to the back and front side seams, and to the sleeve as well.
The neck opening of a woven top must be at least the head circumference, or a short zip or half buttonstand is needed.
A tailored jacket needs interlining to stop sagging or wrinkling, but it must not be so stiff it is uncomfortable.
A jacket lining must not pull or interfere with the fall of the jacket.
Shorten the lining sleeve so the lining does not show at the cuff.
A centre-back tuck in the lining adds comfort and ease.
Cut a pocket flap slightly wider than the pocket so it covers the pocket on both sides.
A pocket hem or facing should be at least 2.5 cm wide.
A skirt zip is normally 20 cm and a trouser zip 18 cm; the skirt must slip over the hips when the zip is open.
Keep a flared hem narrow, about 1 cm or less, to prevent roping when it is stitched.
A six-gored skirt with the zip on the side seam is slimming and allows the centre panels to be cut on the fold.
A centre-back vent is about 3-5 cm deep; the right back takes double the depth for the fold.
A gathered skirt's fullness is set by the hem length, usually about twice the hip measure, and up to three times for more fullness.
A circular skirt's waistline radius comes from the waist measure, adjusted for the type of circle; the formula is given on page 92.
Keep the hem of a circular skirt narrow, about 6 mm, so it does not rope.
The front crotch of a culotte is shorter than the back, so the front is shortened and the back lengthened by the same amount.
On an empire dress, drop the bust point about 3 cm to create the vertical dart, then slash and spread the skirt panels.
A dress's centre-back zip should end about 18-20 cm below the waistline.
After gathering, darting or easing, the bodice and skirt waists must correspond when joined.
With checks or stripes, keep the trouser grainline perpendicular to the hem and match the checks on the outside seams.
Extending the pocket through to the fly holds waist pleats flat over the tummy.
Use calico for pocket facings in denim to reduce bulk over the tummy.
Knitted fleece track pants tend to bag at the knee, so add fullness to the pattern.
Short shorts should fit across the thigh without constriction and end at a flattering point on the leg.
To scale a quarter-scale pattern up to full size, multiply each distance from the bust point by four.
Quarter-scale patterns have no seams or hems; add these after the pattern is complete.
